name: Sunk Cost Escalation Loop
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Throwing Good Qubits After Bad
lesson.summary: The sunk cost escalation loop is a reinforcing loop built from institutional psychology rather than media dynamics: past investment in a particular technical approach makes it progressively harder to abandon, regardless of new evidence, because abandoning it means admitting the earlier investment was wasted.
lesson.body:
Earlier in this book, the sunk cost trap and the sunk cost fallacy were introduced as a psychological bias: the tendency to keep investing in a decision because of what has already been spent, rather than because of what remains to be gained. The sunk cost escalation loop takes that static bias and shows how it becomes dynamic once it is embedded inside a reinforcing feedback structure. A bias that operates once, on one decision, is a mistake. A bias that operates repeatedly, each round making the next round more likely, is a loop, and loops compound.

Here is the mechanism. An institution, a lab, a company, a national program, commits resources to a particular technical approach. That commitment creates stakes: careers are built on the approach succeeding, budgets are justified by its promise, public statements have been made about its viability. Those stakes create pressure to report progress in the most favorable available light, since admitting the approach is underperforming threatens the careers, budgets, and credibility built on top of it. Favorable reporting then supports continued or increased investment, since decision makers reasonably fund what looks like it is working. That increased investment raises the stakes further, deepening the pressure to keep reporting favorably next time. Organizational behavior researchers call this pattern escalation of commitment: people and institutions do not weigh sunk costs once and move on, they get drawn into a spiral where each round of investment makes the next round more psychologically and politically necessary.

Quantum computing offers a live example in the competition between physical qubit modalities: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photonics, neutral atoms, topological approaches, and others. An organization that has spent years and enormous sums building expertise, fabrication facilities, and public identity around one modality faces a genuinely difficult problem if evidence starts suggesting a rival modality is pulling ahead. Switching means writing off specialized talent, custom equipment, and years of institutional narrative, all at once, in public. Staying the course, even once the evidence favors switching, can feel like the safer choice to the people deciding, even though it is often the costlier one in the long run.

This loop is worth distinguishing from the hype reinforcement loop covered in the previous chapter, even though both are reinforcing loops and both can operate on the same underlying technology. The hype loop runs mostly on external perception, media, public excitement, funding optics. The sunk cost escalation loop can run entirely internally, inside a single lab or company, with no press coverage at all, driven purely by the careers and identities of the people closest to the work. A research program can be nearly invisible to the public and still be caught firmly inside a sunk cost escalation loop.

Because this loop is reinforcing, it will not correct itself from the inside, the point made in the general chapter on reinforcing loops. What breaks a sunk cost escalation loop in practice tends to be external: a change in leadership without stakes in the original decision, an independent audit with real authority to redirect funding, or a competing result so unambiguous that favorable framing becomes untenable even to those most invested. That no amount of evidence alone reliably breaks this loop, only structural intervention does, previews the leverage points chapter later in this section.
